Scarf repairs restore higher strength than bonded overlap repairs due to lower adhesive stress concentrations.
Typical scarf taper angles for thick composite repairs are around 3 degrees to keep adhesive shear stress below 30 MPa.
The paper formulates governing differential equations for adhesive shear and peel stresses with variable scarf angle.
A finite difference algorithm is used to solve the governing equations due to singularities at joint ends.
Finite element models use MSC Nastran 2000 and MSC Patran 2003 with plane strain TRIA3 elements for isotropic adherends and WEDGE6 elements for composite adherends.
Adherend thickness in models is about 3 mm; adhesive thickness is 0.2 mm.
Adherend materials modeled include aluminum 7075-T6 and IM7/977-3 carbon epoxy prepreg composite.
Adhesive properties are based on CYTEC FM73 film adhesive.
Optimized scarf angle profiles vary linearly along the joint length to minimize peak adhesive shear stress.
The optimal maximum to minimum scarf angle ratio increases as the modulus ratio between adherends decreases.
Using a low modulus patch reduces adhesive stress by deflecting load away from the adhesive layer.
Adhesive shear stress distributions predicted analytically closely match finite element analysis results.
Ply orientation in composite adherends significantly influences adhesive stress distribution.
The study confirms Hart-Smith's observation that peak adhesive shear stress ratio approaches the adherend modulus ratio in dissimilar adherends.
The optimized scarf repair reduces the amount of undamaged parent material removal compared to conventional scarf repairs.
The study includes sensitivity analyses for isotropic and orthotropic adherend combinations.
The adhesive layer is modeled as a combination of shear and tension spring elements in the analytical formulation.
The scarf joint geometry assumes small adherend thickness compared to length and width.
The study uses boundary conditions where adhesive displacement is zero at one end and matches applied load at the other.
The optimized scarf repair method is applicable to primary composite aircraft structures where damage tolerance is critical.
